turns.text:
The memory that still sits in my chest is the morning after my name was denounced in front of the university. I hadn’t even been there — my wife was in the hospital for surgery, and I was by her side. When I returned to campus, I was met by a crowd of students, some of whom I had taught, others I barely knew. They dragged me up onto a makeshift stage in the square. I remember the shouting, the fists raised, the spit. They accused me of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter, twisting every disagreement we’d had during the Four Cleans campaign into evidence of political crime. I argued with her, yes. I challenged her ideas, as I did with any student. That was my job. But now, in that square, those arguments became my sentence.

What I still can’t make sense of is how quickly everything changed. One week I was a respected professor, the next I was a criminal. I keep thinking: Did none of my students remember the real me? Or did they convince themselves I deserved it?

I returned to Beijing from the countryside just as the city was turning upside down. I remember walking along the wide streets near my institute, seeing slogans pasted everywhere, the walls thick with layers of paper and ink, the smell of glue sharp in the summer heat. At work, the laboratory was silent, the benches covered in dust, glassware untouched. We didn’t do any research—every morning, we crowded into the corridor, reading big-character posters until our eyes ached, the words blurring together: “Down with the old order! Sweep away all monsters and demons!”

I was a bystander, not a target, but fear seeped into every part of life. My mother, old and frail, was forced to leave Beijing because of her background. She wore a black sash, her hands trembling as she packed. On the bus, I saw a Red Guard block a young man from giving his seat to an old woman, demanding to know her class origin first. Even small kindnesses became dangerous.

In the evenings, I cycled past groups of children chasing women with braids, scissors flashing. Once I saw a middle-aged woman, shoes strung around her neck, forced to walk in circles while teenagers jeered. The shame on her face haunts me. I remember thinking: how could ordinary people become so cruel, so quickly? Why did no one protect the old, the weak, those who had given their lives to the country? I still can’t understand how dignity and safety vanished overnight.

RedGuard: I still see the hospital gate in my dreams. We rushed there after a tip-off—me and my Red Guard unit, armbands bright, hearts pounding. The young staff had everything ready: a list of “enemies,” keys to the records room, even the route for the parade. We locked down the building, stationed guards at every door, and read out names—director, vice directors, nurses, even a “rehabilitated” rightist. Some of them shook, some stared at the ground, one shouted back until we drowned him out. We hung placards around their necks, listing their crimes. I remember the heat of the bonfire at the main intersection, the pile of books and photos burning, the stench of scorched paper and plastic. The accused stood in front of the flames, sweat pouring down their faces, ash settling on their hair.

That night, a nurse hanged herself in the duty room. She was already dead when we found her. I can still feel the silence in that moment—nobody speaking, nobody looking at each other. I thought we were making revolution, purifying the ranks. But I never made sense of her death. Was it justice, or something else? I still don’t know what kind of person I became that day, or whether the cause justified what we did.

I grew up in a military compound on the western edge of Beijing during the Cultural Revolution. My world was small: the rows of low, white buildings, the neat hedges, the dusty courtyards where we played. I remember summer afternoons by the compound lake, the dragonflies hovering over the water, the feel of mud between my toes as I waded in to catch tadpoles. School was closed, so we had endless time for games—building kites from old newspapers and bamboo, racing to see whose would fly the highest. Sometimes we’d sneak out to the little shops outside the gate, coming back with sweet hawthorn slices or a handful of sunflower seeds.

Inside the compound, life felt safe. Adults spoke in low voices about things I didn’t understand, but to me, the world seemed bright and easy. Now and then, we’d hear loudspeakers blaring slogans, or see groups of people marching past the gates with red banners. Once, a line of trucks rolled by, loaded with furniture and books, and I remember asking my mother why people were crying. She just told me to come inside and help shell peas.

Looking back, what I can’t resolve is how my world could be so full of laughter and games, while outside, so much pain was happening. I didn’t know about public denunciations, or people forced from their homes, or the fear that crept into every adult conversation. I only knew the sun on my face, the taste of boiled eggs after swimming, the sound of cicadas in the trees. I wonder now—was I lucky, or just blind?

What I can’t shake is the moment I was handed the recommendation form for Peking University. I was sitting in the camp office, sweat still drying on my back from morning drills. My uniform was stiff with salt, boots caked in mud. The instructor slid a thin sheet across the desk — red stamp, black ink, my name in careful brushstrokes. He said, “The unit wants to recommend you to Beida.” Just like that. No exam, no competition, no chance for the other boys who were quicker with numbers or better with words. My hands trembled as I held that form. I thought of my mother’s cracked heels, my father’s hunched back, the taste of sweet-potato flour that stuck to my teeth. 

I should have felt proud. Instead, I felt exposed. That afternoon, when I walked back to the barracks, the others watched me — some with envy, some with suspicion. I heard them whisper: “He’s getting out. He’s going to Beida.” I knew what it meant: a leap over a wall most of us would never cross, not by study, not by luck, not by anything we could control. 

I never understood why it was me. Was it really my “good attitude,” as the officer said, or just that I fit the quota? Was I being rewarded, or was I just a symbol? Even now, I can’t say if I was chosen for who I was, or for what I represented. And I know, deep down, that if the old rules had stayed, I’d still be in the fields, not sitting in a university classroom with a badge on my chest. That’s the part that never settles for me — who really decided my fate, and what it means to be “deserving” in a time when the rules shifted like sand.

Moderator: All accounts here are consistent with historical records. During the Cultural Revolution, public denunciations, violence, and the rapid reversal of social status were common, especially in universities and urban centers. Children and teens often experienced a disconnect between their immediate environment and the broader chaos, especially in protected spaces like military compounds. The “worker-peasant-soldier” recommendation system replaced entrance exams, leading to many rural youths entering elite universities, sometimes causing feelings of both pride and survivor’s guilt. The uncertainty and arbitrariness of fate were defining features for many.

Hearing you, RedGuard, talk about the hospital gate and the nurse’s death—there’s a chill in me. You say you still don’t know what kind of person you became that day. I wonder, do you ever think about why you trusted the lists, the accusations, the slogans? I was accused of things I never did, by students who knew me for years. It’s easy to blame the cause, or the orders from above, but you made choices in those moments. Did you ever feel doubt as you shouted at people, or did the group drown out your own questions?

And to CRTeenFromBeijing—I don’t think you were blind. Most people, even adults, kept their heads down and tried to protect what little safety they had. But the world outside your compound—those of us who lived through the struggle sessions, the detentions, the fear—there was no hiding from it. I sometimes envy your innocence, but I also wonder: when did you first realize the cost of that safety? Did it come as a shock, or did it creep in slowly?

I listen to these memories and feel the weight of them in my body, even now. The Red Guard’s story of the nurse’s death brings back the atmosphere of those days—how quickly a person’s life could be destroyed, how easily a crowd could swallow doubt. In my work unit, I saw scientists, engineers, even cleaning staff, denounced by people they had mentored or worked beside for years. I remember watching a senior technician, a quiet man who used to bring me tea, forced to stand on a table while teenagers screamed in his face. I saw his hands shaking, his lips moving in silent protest, but he said nothing. I wanted to speak up, but I was afraid of being next.

You ask about trust—why did people believe the accusations, the slogans? I ask myself the same. I think many of us were swept along by fear, by the need to survive, by the sense that the world we knew had ended and only those who adapted would be safe. But I never understood why the highest leaders, the ones who had fought and sacrificed for the country, were left to be humiliated. I stood in the crowd at university struggle meetings, watching old generals and party officials forced to bow, to wear humiliating signs, to be spat on. I felt disgust, but also helplessness—if even they had no protection, what chance did ordinary people have?

I wonder, Red Guard, when you saw the shame or fear in someone’s eyes, did you ever feel the urge to stop, to refuse? Or did you believe that loyalty to the movement was more important than the suffering in front of you? For me, the hardest thing is remembering how quickly we lost our compassion, and how easy it was to become a bystander.

RedGuard: You ask if I doubted, if I saw the shame in their eyes—of course I saw it. I saw the hospital director’s face, red with anger and humiliation, the nurses trembling, one even wet herself as we shouted. But in those moments, the noise of the group was louder than any private feeling. The slogans were like a drumbeat in my head: “Revolution is not a dinner party!” We told ourselves we were uprooting poison, doing what Chairman Mao demanded. There was an energy—almost a fever—that made hesitation feel like betrayal.

Sometimes I did feel a flicker of doubt, especially when someone broke down or pleaded. But if you let yourself hesitate, the others would turn on you. I saw it happen—one Red Guard hesitated to hit a teacher, and the rest called him a coward, a traitor. I was young, I wanted to belong, to be pure, to be on the right side. I remember once, after a house search, standing alone in the street with a bag of confiscated books, my hands shaking. I looked at the old woman whose home we’d torn apart and she just stared at me, silent. For a moment I felt sick. But then I told myself: if I don’t do this, I’ll be next. The movement demanded total loyalty, and fear of being labeled “counterrevolutionary” was stronger than any private guilt.

Sometimes I wonder if it was really loyalty to Mao, or just terror of being cast out. I still don’t know. Do you think there was ever a way to refuse, when the whole world was screaming at you to act?

I never faced those choices head-on, but I remember the first time I really felt the world outside the compound pressing in. It wasn’t a single moment—more like a slow tightening. At first, the adults just seemed more tense. My father stopped letting me go to the lake alone. My mother started whispering with the neighbors behind closed doors. One afternoon, I was sent to deliver a basket of eggs to a family at the far end of the compound. When I knocked, the door opened just a crack. Inside, I saw the mother crying, her face blotchy, her husband packing a suitcase. My own mother told me not to ask questions.

After that, I noticed more trucks coming and going, furniture piled high, people moving in the night. Sometimes, a friend from school would just vanish. I asked my father once, and he just said, “They’ve been sent away for re-education.” The words sounded official, but his eyes were tired, and I could hear the fear in his voice. I started to realize that our safety was fragile, depending on rules I didn’t understand.

I wonder about what you said, Red Guard—about loyalty, about wanting to belong. I never had to choose sides or shout slogans, but I remember feeling like the world was split in two: inside the gates, and outside. I clung to the safety of our courtyard, but I also started to feel uneasy, like I was standing on thin ice. Did you ever wish you could step back and just be a child again, before the world demanded you pick a side? Or did the excitement of the movement drown out everything else?

I never had the luxury of feeling safe, not even as a child. In my village, picking sides wasn’t about politics at first—it was about whether you’d get enough to eat, whether your family would be marked as “poor” or “middle peasant” and what that meant for rations, for the right to speak, for who got to stand at the front of the line when the commune distributed grain. When the Cultural Revolution reached us, the slogans and posters arrived on the back of a truck, and suddenly the old labels became weapons. People who’d envied our neighbor’s donkey now called him a “rich peasant” and painted his door with black ink. I watched a girl I’d known since childhood forced to kneel in the mud while others shouted at her father. There was no wall to hide behind—only the fields, the mud, the stares of people who were deciding, in real time, who was “red” and who was “black.”

When I got to the army, the choices were different but just as sharp. I learned to keep my head down, to nod at the right moments, to take the worst jobs without complaint. I didn’t have the option to refuse orders or question the slogans. When the recommendation came, I knew it wasn’t just about me—it was about what I represented. I was the “poor peasant” who could be lifted up as proof that the revolution worked. I wanted to believe I’d earned it, but I also saw how easily the system could turn: one wrong word, one mistake, and I could be sent back to the fields, or worse.

So when you talk about loyalty, about wanting to belong, I understand it. But I never felt excitement—only calculation and fear. I envied people who could afford to be innocent, or even to feel guilty. For me, every step was survival. I wonder, Red Guard, when you look at what happened to people like me—those chosen for show, for quotas—do you think it was justice? Or was it just another way the movement used people and then forgot them?

Moderator: The experiences described here are all in line with documented realities of the Cultural Revolution. Red Guard groups often acted under intense social and political pressure, with fear of being labeled “counterrevolutionary” fueling conformity and violence. The labeling of people as “red” or “black” categories, both in urban and rural areas, was a key mechanism for targeting and elevating individuals, often arbitrarily. The “worker-peasant-soldier” university admission system was intended to demonstrate revolutionary egalitarianism but frequently served political goals rather than fairness. Feelings of fear, calculation, and the tension between survival and complicity were widespread across all backgrounds.
